content.statement: A GET request should not change data on the server.

remember: GET is a safe method: crawlers, prefetchers and retries send it freely, so changes belong in POST, PUT, PATCH or DELETE.

content.prompt: POST /api/users has just created a new user. Which status code fits the response best?

remember: 201 Created says a new resource now exists; its URL goes in the Location header.

content.prompt: Match each status code with its meaning.

right.text: The target resource does not exist
An unexpected failure on the server
Success, with no body to return
A new resource was made

remember: 2xx means success, 4xx means the client's request is at fault, 5xx means the server failed.

content.prompt: Three of these need a changed request to succeed. Which one may succeed if the same request is retried later?

items.text: 400 Bad Request
415 Unsupported Media Type
413 Content Too Large
503 Service Unavailable

remember: 503 is a temporary server problem worth retrying later; a 400, 413 or 415 fails again until the request changes.

content.prompt: A client sends PUT /docs/7 with If-Match: "v3", but another user has already saved version "v4". What should the server answer?

remember: When an If-Match condition fails, the server skips the change and answers 412; that is how HTTP prevents lost updates.

content.statement: In a REST API, GET, PUT and DELETE can all be sent to the same URL, such as /orders/7.

remember: One URL names one resource; the method says whether to read, replace or delete it.

content.prompt: What do the query parameters in GET /api/orders?status=open&sort=-created do?

options.text: Filter and sort the list of orders
Create a new order with status open
Update every order that is still open
Select a different version of the API

remember: Query parameters narrow, sort and page a collection; they never turn a GET into a change.

content.prompt: Three of these URLs follow REST naming. Which one does not?

items.text: /users/42/orders
/getUserOrders?id=42
/orders/17
/products/9/reviews

remember: REST URLs are nouns for resources; the verb belongs in the HTTP method, not in the path.

content.prompt: Fill the blank so the client learns the URL of the order it just created.
content.code:
POST /api/orders HTTP/1.1
Content-Type: application/json

{"productId": 5, "quantity": 2}

HTTP/1.1 201 Created
____: /api/orders/981

remember: A 201 response names the new resource's URL in the Location header.

content.prompt: Match each request with what it does in a REST API.

right.text: Change only the fields sent in the body
Remove order 7
Create a new order
Replace order 7 with the body

remember: POST creates in a collection, PUT replaces the whole resource, PATCH changes part of it, DELETE removes it.

content.statement: If the frontend form already validates the input, the API can trust the data it receives.

remember: Anyone can call the API directly with curl or a script, so the server validates every input itself.

content.prompt: POST /api/users receives {"email": "not-an-email"}. What should the API do?

options.text: Save the user and let them fix the email later
Answer 400 and name the invalid field
Answer 500, because the data is broken
Drop the email and save the rest

remember: Bad input is the client's mistake: reject it with 400 and say which field is wrong, before doing any work.

content.prompt: What does this print?

remember: Collect every field error and return them together, so the client can fix them all in one go.

content.prompt: A customer ordered a quantity of -5 and was credited money instead of charged. Find the bug.

fixes.text: Convert quantity with parseInt before the check
Validate productId before loading the product
Also reject quantity < 1 in the condition

remember: Check both ends of a numeric range; a check for 'too large' alone lets zero and negative values through.

content.prompt: A sort column cannot be passed as a query parameter, so it goes into the SQL text. Fill the blank so the endpoint is safe from SQL injection.

remember: Values that cannot be bound as parameters, like a sort column, must match an allow-list of known values.

content.statement: A 500 response should include the exception's stack trace so client developers can debug faster.

remember: Log the stack trace on the server and send the client only a generic message plus an id it can quote.

content.prompt: Why should every endpoint return errors in the same body shape, such as Problem Details?

options.text: Errors in one shape are smaller and faster to send
Browsers reject error bodies in any other format
It lets the server skip setting a status code
Clients can handle every error with one piece of code

remember: One error shape across all endpoints means one error handler on every client.

content.prompt: While the database was down, the dashboard of 5xx responses stayed at zero and the app, which checks response.ok, showed "Saved". Find the bug.

fixes.text: Send the error with res.status(500).json(...)
Log the error after sending the response
Send err.message instead of "save failed"

remember: A failure needs a failing status code; a 200 with an error in the body looks like success to clients and monitoring.

content.prompt: What does this print?
content.code:
class AppError(Exception): pass
class NotFound(AppError): pass
class Conflict(AppError): pass

STATUS = [
    (AppError, 500),
    (NotFound, 404),
    (Conflict, 409),
]

def status_for(err):
    for cls, status in STATUS:
        if isinstance(err, cls):
            return status
    return 500

print(status_for(NotFound()), status_for(KeyError()))

remember: Check the most specific error types first; a base class checked first matches every subclass.

content.prompt: Sign-up fails: the e-mail is already taken. Which of these belongs only in the server log, not in the response?

items.text: The status code 409
A trace id the user can quote to support
The name of the unique index the INSERT violated
The field that caused the error: email

remember: Translate internal failures such as a violated index into client terms like 'e-mail already taken'; schema details stay in the log.

content.statement: A 401 Unauthorized response means the user is signed in but may not perform this action.

remember: 401 means the server does not know who you are; 403 means it knows and still says no.

content.prompt: Which of these checks is authorization rather than authentication?

options.text: Comparing the password with the stored hash
Verifying the signature of a JWT
Looking up the session id from the cookie
Checking that the user owns the invoice they asked for

remember: Authentication answers who is calling; authorization answers whether that caller may do this particular thing.

content.prompt: Order the steps of a password login that uses a server-side session.

steps.text: The server stores a new session with a random id
The browser sends the cookie with every later request
The client sends the e-mail and password over HTTPS
The server compares the password with the stored hash
The server returns the session id in an HttpOnly cookie

remember: Verify the password, create the session, hand back only its id in an HttpOnly cookie, and look it up on every request.

content.prompt: Match each item with its role in authentication.

right.text: Short-lived credential sent with every API call
Stops page JavaScript from reading the cookie
Stored instead of the password itself
Longer-lived secret used only to get new access tokens

remember: Store hashes, not passwords; keep access tokens short-lived and renew them with a separate refresh token.

content.prompt: Any signed-in customer can read other customers' invoices by changing the id in the URL. Find the bug.

fixes.text: Return 403 instead of 404 when no invoice is found
Add AND customer_id = $2 and pass req.user.id
Switch invoice ids from numbers to random UUIDs

remember: Being signed in is not permission: scope every lookup to what the caller owns, or anyone can walk the ids.

content.statement: Middleware runs in the order it was registered, so its position in the pipeline matters.

remember: Middleware runs in registration order; anything a handler depends on must be registered before it.

content.prompt: In an Express-style app, the authentication middleware is registered after the route handlers. What happens to a request for a protected route?

options.text: The handler answers without checking who is calling
The framework moves authentication to the front
The request hangs until it times out

remember: Middleware only guards what comes after it; register authentication before the routes it protects.

content.prompt: What does this print?

remember: Middleware wraps the rest of the pipeline: code after await next() runs on the way back out, in reverse order.

content.prompt: Every request, even GET /api/health, hangs until the client times out. Find the bug.

fixes.text: Register express.json() before this middleware
Mark the middleware function as async
Call next() after setting req.startedAt

remember: A middleware must either send a response or call next(); doing neither leaves the request hanging.

content.prompt: A browser app on another origin calls this API with a bearer token. Order the middleware from first to run to last.

steps.text: Authorization: checks the user's role
Route handler
CORS: answers preflight OPTIONS requests
Authentication: validates the token, sets the user

remember: CORS goes before authentication, because the browser's preflight request carries no token and would get 401.

content.statement: Sending DELETE /api/orders/7 twice leaves the server in the same state as sending it once.

remember: DELETE is idempotent: the second call may answer 404, but the state is the same as after the first.

content.prompt: Which of these requests is not idempotent?

remember: Idempotency depends on what a request does: setting a value is safe to repeat, adding to it is not.

content.prompt: An app sends POST /payments and the connection drops before the response arrives. How can it retry without risking a double charge?

options.text: Retry with the same Idempotency-Key header; the server replays the stored result
Retry as PUT /payments, because PUT is idempotent
Wait 30 seconds so the first request can finish, then retry
Send a fresh random id with each retry so the server can tell them apart

remember: An idempotency key lets the server recognise a retry and replay its stored response instead of doing the work again.

content.prompt: What does this print?

remember: Check-then-act with an await in between lets concurrent duplicates through; claim the key atomically before doing the work.

content.prompt: Order what the server does with a POST /payments request that carries an Idempotency-Key.

steps.text: Charge the card
Look up the key; if a finished response is stored, return it
Send the response to the client
No stored response: claim the key by inserting it as in progress
Save the status code and body under the key

remember: Claim the key before the work and save the response before sending it, so every retry finds the claim or the stored result.

content.statement: When a client asks for limit=1000000, the API should return that many rows.

remember: The server enforces a maximum page size; a client cannot use a huge limit to download the whole table at once.

content.prompt: GET /api/products could return two million rows. What is the usual fix?

options.text: Return one page at a time, with a limit and a way to get the next page
Compress the response so the two million rows download faster
Raise the server timeout so the query has time to finish
Keep the full two-million-row response cached in memory

remember: Large lists are returned in pages of bounded size, with a way to ask for the next one.

content.prompt: Page 1 is fetched, a new row is inserted, then page 2 is fetched. What does this print?

remember: With offset pagination, a row inserted before the current position pushes the others down, so the next page repeats a row.

content.prompt: Posts are listed newest first. :last_id is the id of the last post on the previous page. Fill the blank to get the next page.
content.code:
SELECT id, title
FROM posts
WHERE id ____ :last_id
ORDER BY id DESC
LIMIT 20;

remember: A cursor continues from the last row seen in the sort direction: with ORDER BY id DESC the next page has smaller ids.

content.prompt: A bulk import gave thousands of orders the same created_at. Some of those orders never appear on any page. Find the bug.
content.code:
def next_page(db, cursor):
    # cursor: created_at of the last order shown
    return db.fetch_all(
        """
        SELECT id, created_at, total
        FROM orders
        WHERE created_at < %(cursor)s
        ORDER BY created_at DESC
        LIMIT 50
        """,
        {"cursor": cursor},
    )

fixes.text: Use <= instead of < in the WHERE clause
Raise the LIMIT so all tied rows fit on one page
Sort and compare on (created_at, id) and keep both in the cursor

remember: A cursor needs a unique sort key; add the id as a tie-breaker, or rows that share a timestamp get skipped.

content.statement: A rate limiter that rejects a request should answer with 500 Internal Server Error.

remember: Over the limit is answered with 429 Too Many Requests, ideally with Retry-After saying when to come back.

content.prompt: What is the main reason to rate-limit a login endpoint?

options.text: To slow down attackers who guess passwords
To make each successful login faster
To remove the need for hashing passwords
To make sure no login request ever fails

remember: Limiting attempts per client or account makes brute-force password guessing too slow to work.

content.prompt: Fill the blank so the client knows how many seconds to wait.
content.code:
HTTP/1.1 429 Too Many Requests
Content-Type: application/problem+json
____: 30

{"title": "Too many requests"}

remember: Retry-After on a 429 tells the client how long to wait, in seconds or as a date.

content.prompt: The limit is 3 requests per minute. What does this print?

remember: A fixed window resets at its boundary, so a client can send twice the limit within seconds around the edge.

content.prompt: Match each rate-limiting algorithm with its behaviour.

right.text: Refills at a steady rate and allows bursts up to its capacity
Lets queued requests out at a constant rate, smoothing bursts
Stores a timestamp per request: exact, but memory grows with traffic
One counter per period: cheap, but bursty at the period edge

remember: Fixed windows are cheap but bursty at the edge, sliding logs are exact but costly, buckets trade burst size against a steady rate.

content.statement: A cached value updates itself automatically when the database row it came from changes.

remember: A cache does not watch your database; a value stays stale until its TTL runs out or your code deletes it on write.

content.prompt: Building the leaderboard takes 2 seconds and every request asks for it. What does a server-side cache add?

options.text: It keeps the built leaderboard so later requests reuse it until it expires
It makes the database run the 2-second query faster
It stores a copy of the leaderboard in each player's browser
It builds every possible leaderboard when the server starts

remember: A cache stores a computed result so repeated requests skip the expensive work until the value expires.

content.prompt: Order the steps of a cache-aside read when the value is not cached yet.

steps.text: Store the value in the cache with a TTL
Look the key up in the cache and miss
Return the value to the caller
Build the cache key from the request
Load the value from the database

remember: Cache-aside: check the cache, on a miss load from the database, store the result with a TTL, then return it.

content.prompt: What does this print?

remember: Until its TTL runs out, a cached value hides changes in the database; pick the TTL by how stale the data may be.

content.prompt: Under load, a renamed user sometimes shows the old name for up to an hour. Find the bug.

fixes.text: Lower the TTL in getUser to 60 seconds
Delete the cache entry after the database update
Run the delete and the update together with Promise.all

remember: Delete the cached value after the write; deleting first lets a concurrent read cache the old row again for a full TTL.

content.statement: Moving slow work such as sending e-mail to a background queue lets the API respond without waiting for it.

remember: Put slow side work on a queue and answer the request right away; a worker does the rest.

content.prompt: Your queue delivers every job at least once, so a job may run twice. What must the job handler be?

options.text: Idempotent, so a second run changes nothing
Fast enough to finish within the request timeout
Running on the same server as the API
Wrapped in a try/catch that hides every error

remember: At-least-once delivery means duplicates happen; write jobs so running them twice does no extra harm.

content.prompt: Three of these tasks are good candidates for a background job. Which one should stay in the request?

items.text: Sending the order confirmation e-mail
Checking the password during login
Resizing an uploaded photo into thumbnails
Generating a yearly PDF report

remember: Work the response depends on stays in the request; work the user can wait for goes to a queue.

content.prompt: If reserving stock fails, the order is rolled back, but the customer still gets a receipt e-mail. Find the bug.

fixes.text: Enqueue the job after tx.commit() succeeds
Delay the job by 5 seconds so the transaction can finish
Wrap queue.add in its own try/catch

remember: Enqueue a job only after the transaction commits, or use an outbox; otherwise workers act on data that was rolled back.

content.prompt: Order the steps of the transactional outbox pattern for sending an order e-mail.

steps.text: A relay reads the outbox row and puts the job on the queue
Commit the transaction
Begin a database transaction
A worker takes the job and sends the e-mail
Insert the order and an outbox row in the same transaction

remember: With an outbox, the job is saved in the same transaction as the data, so it exists exactly when the data does.

content.statement: When changing one module regularly forces changes in several others, those modules are tightly coupled.

remember: Modules that keep changing together are coupled; loosen them so each can change on its own.

content.prompt: In a layered backend (API, Application, Domain, Infrastructure), which dependency breaks the rule that dependencies point inward?

options.text: An endpoint calls a use case from the application layer
The Order domain class imports the Postgres client to save itself
Infrastructure implements an interface the application layer defines
A use case creates and changes Order objects from the domain

remember: The domain depends on nothing; databases and frameworks sit at the edge and depend inward on it.

content.prompt: Match each coupling smell with the change that loosens it.

left.text: A service reads another module's tables directly
Business rules live inside HTTP handlers
A class creates its own database client with new
Endpoints return database entities as they are

right.text: Pass the client in through the constructor
Map entities to response DTOs
Call that module's public API instead
Move the rules into a use case the handler calls

remember: Use other modules' public APIs, inject dependencies, keep rules out of handlers and map entities to DTOs.

content.prompt: Fill the blank so the orders module needs no change when another module starts reacting to new orders.

remember: Publishing a fact like order.placed lets new consumers subscribe without touching the publisher; a command names its receiver.

content.prompt: Three of these tightly couple services A and B. Which one does not?

items.text: B reads A's tables in A's database
A calls B over HTTP and fails while B is down
A and B share a library of database entities
B consumes A's versioned events and keeps its own copy

remember: Shared databases, shared entity libraries and synchronous call chains couple services; versioned events with local copies keep them apart.

content.statement: A HEAD request asks for the same response as GET, but the server sends back only the headers and no body.

remember: HEAD is GET without the body: a cheap way to check that a resource exists or read its headers without downloading it.

content.prompt: The URL /api/countries only supports GET. A client sends DELETE /api/countries. Which status code fits the response?

remember: 405 means the URL exists but does not support that method; the Allow header lists the methods that work.

content.prompt: GET /api/orders?status=refunded runs without errors, but no order matches the filter. What should the API return?

options.text: 404 Not Found with an error message
400 Bad Request with an error message

remember: A search with no matches still succeeded: return 200 with [], so clients show 'no results' instead of handling an error.

content.prompt: Three of these confirm that the server has finished the work the request asked for. Which one does not?

items.text: 201 Created
204 No Content
200 OK
202 Accepted

remember: 202 Accepted means the work was queued, not done; the client checks a status URL later to learn the outcome.

content.prompt: In Express. This endpoint only reads JSON bodies, and a client posts the order as XML. Fill the blank.

remember: 415 rejects a request body in a format the server cannot read; 406 means it cannot produce the format the Accept header asks for.

content.prompt: In a browser or Node.js, what does this print?

remember: A 204 is a success with no body, so res.json() throws; check for 204 before parsing the response.

content.prompt: In Express. When the report has not changed, the browser should reuse its cached copy, but users see an empty report instead. Find the bug.

fixes.text: Compare against If-Match instead of If-None-Match
Answer with res.status(304).end() instead
Set the ETag header after the if block

remember: A matching If-None-Match gets 304 Not Modified, which tells the browser to reuse its copy; a 200 with no body replaces it.

content.prompt: An API runs behind a reverse proxy such as nginx. Match each situation with the status code the client receives.

left.text: A bug in the app throws; the app's error handler replies
The app is still working when the proxy stops waiting
The app replies with bytes the proxy cannot parse as HTTP
The app is in maintenance mode and says to retry later

right.text: 504 Gateway Timeout
503 Service Unavailable
500 Internal Server Error
502 Bad Gateway

remember: 500 comes from the app itself; 502 and 504 come from the proxy when the app's reply is broken or too slow; 503 says retry later.

content.prompt: A client uploads a 2 GB file with POST and the header Expect: 100-continue. Order the exchange when the upload succeeds.

steps.text: Client sends the 2 GB body
Server answers 100 Continue
Client sends the request headers only
Server answers 201 Created
Server checks the headers: token, Content-Length

remember: With Expect: 100-continue the body waits for 100 Continue, so the server can refuse a too-large or unauthorised upload before it is sent.

content.statement: When a POST gets a 307 Temporary Redirect, the browser follows it by sending a GET to the new URL.

remember: 307 and 308 repeat the same method and body at the new URL; only 301, 302 and 303 let a browser turn a POST into a GET.

content.statement: A REST API must send and receive its data as JSON.

remember: REST does not fix a data format; JSON is common, and the Content-Type header says which format a body uses.

content.prompt: GET /users returns the collection and GET /users/:id one user. What does this print?

remember: A plural path like /users names the whole collection; adding an id, as in /users/2, names one member of it.

content.prompt: PUT /api/users/7 should update user 7. A request whose body still said "id": 8 changed user 8 instead. Find the bug.

fixes.text: Convert id with Number(id) before the lookup
Take id from req.params.id, not from req.body
Look the user up by email instead of by id

remember: The URL identifies the resource: take the id from the path and never let a field in the body redirect the write.

content.prompt: Match each piece of information with where it belongs in a REST request.

left.text: The id of the order to read
The fields of a new order
The format the client wants back

right.text: The query string
The Accept header
The URL path
The request body

remember: The path names the resource, the query string filters it, the body carries its data and the Accept header picks the format.

content.prompt: Building a CSV export takes minutes, so the API runs it as a job. Order what happens, from first to last.

steps.text: Client sends GET /exports/jobs/5 and sees status running
Client sends GET /exports/77 and downloads the file
Client sends POST /exports with the export options
Worker finishes and the job now links to /exports/77
Server queues the job and answers 202 with /exports/jobs/5

remember: Slow work gets 202 Accepted and a job resource to poll; when the job is done, that resource points to the result.

content.statement: PUT /api/users/42 can create user 42 when it does not exist yet; the server then answers 201 Created.

remember: PUT stores the body at the URL the client names: it replaces the resource there, or creates it with 201 if it was missing.

content.prompt: An admin, who may read every order, calls GET /api/users/42/orders/9. Order 9 exists but belongs to user 17. What should the API answer?

options.text: 200 with order 9, since the admin may read it
404 Not Found, since user 42 has no order 9
403 Forbidden, since order 9 is not user 42's
400 Bad Request, since the two ids do not match

remember: A nested URL scopes the lookup: /users/42/orders/9 exists only if order 9 belongs to user 42; otherwise it is a 404.

content.prompt: User 42 has the nickname "ana99". A client sends PATCH /api/users/42 with Content-Type: application/merge-patch+json and the body {"nickname": null}. What happens to the nickname?

options.text: It keeps ana99, since null means no change
The patch is rejected with 400 Bad Request
It is stored as the JSON value null
It is removed from the user resource

remember: In JSON Merge Patch, null deletes the field, so a merge patch cannot set a value to null; a JSON Patch replace can.

content.prompt: Three of these changes to a public JSON API can break clients that work today. Which one cannot?

items.text: Let numeric ids grow past 2^53 in JSON
Make a required request field optional
Return null in a field that was never null
Start rejecting quantity above 100

remember: Accepting more is safe; tightening input, adding nulls or sending numbers a JavaScript client cannot hold exactly breaks clients.

content.prompt: GET /api/reports/5 returns JSON or CSV depending on Accept. A CDN served a cached CSV to a client that asked for JSON. Fill the blank so the CDN caches the two apart.
content.code:
GET /api/reports/5 HTTP/1.1
Accept: text/csv

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: text/csv
Cache-Control: public, max-age=300
____

remember: When a response depends on a request header such as Accept, list it in Vary, or caches hand one client's format to another.

content.statement: An API should validate a request's input before it writes anything to the database.

remember: Validate first and answer 400 before any write, so a rejected request leaves no half-saved data behind.

content.statement: If a request body parses as valid JSON, the API can treat its contents as valid input.

remember: Valid JSON only means the body parses; the server still checks each field's presence, type and range.

content.prompt: The profile form only has a name field, yet a user sent {"name": "Ana", "role": "admin"} to this endpoint and became an admin. What is the right fix?

options.text: Check that name is a non-empty string
Copy only allowed fields, such as name, into user
Leave role out of the JSON the endpoint returns
Accept only requests whose Origin is the app's site

remember: Copy only the fields an endpoint allows; assigning the whole body lets a client set fields like role that no form ever showed.

content.prompt: In an Express app, a client calls GET /api/products?limit=abc. What does the check on line 3 do?

options.text: Rejects it, because "abc" is not a number
Throws a TypeError for comparing a string to a number
Lets it through, because NaN > 100 is false

remember: Query parameters arrive as strings: parse and type-check them before range checks, because NaN fails every comparison.

content.prompt: Three of these sign-up checks are decided by the request's own data. Which one can pass for two concurrent requests and still let bad data in?

items.text: email has a valid address format
password is at least 12 characters
displayName has 3 to 30 characters
username is not taken by another user

remember: A check against other rows, like a free username, races between requests; back it with a unique constraint in the database.

content.prompt: In JavaScript, fill the blank so the check passes only a complete order code such as ORD-1234.

remember: Anchor validation regexes at both ends with ^ and $ and no m flag, or a value that merely contains a valid code passes.

content.prompt: What does this print?

remember: Normalize first (trim, lowercase), then validate the value you will store; checking the raw input lets short or blank values through.

content.prompt: Avatars may only be downloaded over HTTPS from the host img.example.com, yet the server fetched a file from an attacker's server. Find the bug.

fixes.text: Lowercase url before the startsWith check
Parse it with new URL() and check protocol and hostname
Also require url to end in .png or .jpg

remember: Parse structured input such as a URL before checking it; a prefix check passes img.example.com.evil.net and img.example.com@evil.net.

content.prompt: PATCH /api/profile takes a JSON merge patch. nickname is optional; when present it must be a string of 3-20 characters. Match each body with the result.

right.text: Nickname is removed
400: nickname must be a string
Nickname stays as it was
400: nickname must be 3-20 characters

remember: In a partial update a missing field means leave it and null means clear it; bind and validate the two cases separately.

content.prompt: GET /files/{name} serves files from /srv/files. Order the steps so ../ tricks, even percent-encoded ones, cannot reach files outside it.

steps.text: Check the resolved path starts with /srv/files/
Stream the file's bytes to the client
Percent-decode the name from the request URL
Open the file, or answer 404 if it is missing
Resolve /srv/files plus the name to an absolute path

remember: Validate the canonical form: decode and resolve a path first, then check it is inside the allowed directory before touching the disk.

content.statement: Problem Details (application/problem+json) is a standard JSON format for describing errors in HTTP API responses.

remember: Problem Details is the standard error body for HTTP APIs: fields such as type, title, status and detail in one predictable shape.

content.prompt: Fill the blank so the client learns nothing about what failed inside the server.

remember: Send clients a fixed, generic message for unexpected errors; the exception's message and stack belong in the server log.

content.prompt: An endpoint builds its error body like this. What does this print?

remember: JSON.stringify turns an Error into {} because message and stack are not enumerable; copy the fields you want to send into a plain object.

content.prompt: Missing records should get a 404 with their message; every other failure must reach the client only as a generic 500. Find the bug.

fixes.text: Use err.status ?? 500 instead of a fixed 500
Replace err.message with a fixed generic title
Move err.message from title into a detail field

remember: Show the message only for errors you raise on purpose for the client; unexpected errors get a generic body and their details go to the log.

content.prompt: Match each Problem Details field with what it holds.

right.text: An explanation specific to this one occurrence
A URI that identifies this one occurrence
A URI that identifies the kind of problem
A short summary that is the same for every occurrence

remember: In Problem Details, type and title describe the kind of problem and stay fixed; detail and instance describe this one occurrence.

content.prompt: Placing an order fails because the product has just sold out. Order what happens, from the database to the user.

steps.text: The global error handler maps OutOfStockError to 409
PostgreSQL rejects the UPDATE: the stock >= 0 check fails
The app shows 'Sold out' on the product page
The data layer catches the driver error, throws OutOfStockError
The client receives a Problem Details body titled 'Out of stock'

remember: Translate low-level errors into domain errors near their source, so the error handler maps meaning to status codes without knowing SQL.

content.statement: Once a server has sent part of a 200 response body, it can still change the status to 500 if a later step fails.

remember: The status line goes out before the body; once streaming has started, a server can only abort the connection to signal failure.

content.prompt: Your API calls a payment provider, which answers 401 because your API's own provider key has expired. What should your API answer its client?

options.text: 502, because a dependency behind the API failed
401, passing on the provider's status unchanged
403, because the payment was not authorized
400, because the request could not be processed

remember: Never forward a dependency's status as your own: its 401 tells your client that the client's login failed. Answer 5xx and log the cause.

content.prompt: A browser app on another origin calls your API. Successful calls work, but when the API answers 500, fetch rejects with a TypeError instead of giving the app the response. Why?

options.text: fetch rejects its promise for every 5xx status
Browsers hide 5xx bodies from scripts on other origins
The 500 response has no Access-Control-Allow-Origin header
The preflight check rejects the problem+json content type

remember: Error responses need CORS headers too; without them the browser hides a 500 from the app as a network error.

content.prompt: Three of these let an attacker learn whether an account or record exists. Which one does not?

items.text: Login says 'wrong password' only for registered e-mails
Other users' orders get 403, missing orders get 404
Password reset replies faster for unknown e-mails
A 400 names the request field that failed validation

remember: Give the same status, message and timing whether or not a record exists; any difference lets attackers enumerate accounts and ids.

content.statement: A password plus a one-time code from an authenticator app on your phone counts as two-factor authentication.

remember: Two-factor means two different kinds of proof, such as something you know (a password) and something you have (a phone).

content.prompt: DELETE /api/posts/7 arrives with a bearer token. Put the server's steps in order.

steps.text: Check that this user may delete post 7
Read the token from the Authorization header
Delete the post and answer 204
Verify the token to learn who the user is

remember: Authenticate first to learn who is calling, then check that this caller may do this exact action, and only then do the work.

content.statement: Over HTTPS, sending the access token in the URL, as in /api/me?token=abc, is as safe as sending it in the Authorization header.

remember: URLs end up in server logs, browser history and Referer headers, so send tokens in the Authorization header, never in the query string.

content.prompt: An SPA uses 15-minute access tokens and a 30-day refresh token. An API call returns 401 because the access token has just expired. What should the app do?

options.text: Sign the user out, because the refresh token expired with it
Retry the same call a few times with the same access token
Get a new access token with the refresh token, then retry
Send the refresh token as the bearer token on the same call

remember: An expired access token is renewed with the refresh token behind the scenes; the user signs in again only when that refresh fails.

content.prompt: Access tokens last 15 minutes; the API checks only their signature and expiry. Refresh tokens last 30 days; the refresh endpoint rejects banned users. After a ban, how long can the user still call the API?

options.text: Up to 15 minutes, until their access token expires
Not at all; the ban applies from their next request
Up to 30 days, until their refresh token expires
Until they sign out on their own device

remember: A self-contained access token cannot be recalled: a ban or role change reaches the API only when the token expires and must be refreshed.

content.prompt: Three of these let an attacker find out which e-mail addresses have an account. Which one does not?

items.text: Login replies "No account uses this e-mail"
Password reset gives the same reply at the same speed for any e-mail
Login replies in 5 ms for unknown e-mails and 300 ms for known ones
Sign-up replies "This e-mail is already registered"

remember: Answer the same way at the same speed whether or not an account exists, or the login, sign-up and reset forms become an account finder.

content.prompt: After login the browser is redirected to the ?next= value. Fill the blank so next can never send the user to another site.

remember: Parse the redirect target and compare its whole origin: prefix checks miss //evil.example and suffix checks miss evilshop.example.

content.prompt: Refresh tokens are rotated and a reused one revokes its whole family. What does this print?

remember: With rotation and reuse detection, two tabs refreshing at once look like theft and log the user out; let tabs share one refresh call.

content.prompt: Before sending the user to the provider, /auth/start saved a random state in req.session.oauthState. Attackers get victims signed in to the attacker's own account. Find the bug.

fixes.text: Also reject a state shorter than 32 characters
Also reject when state differs from req.session.oauthState
Pass state to exchangeCode so the provider checks it

remember: The OAuth state must match the value saved in this browser's session; checking only that it is present lets an attacker's callback log you in.

content.prompt: The API runs on several instances behind a load balancer. Match each production symptom with its cause.

left.text: Cookie sessions are lost at random, but never when only one instance runs
JWTs issued by one instance fail the signature check on another
One instance rejects freshly issued tokens as not yet valid
After login, the SPA on app.shop.example gets 401 from api.shop.example

right.text: fetch is called without credentials: "include"
That instance's clock runs a few minutes behind
Each instance creates its own signing key at startup
Session data is kept in each instance's memory

remember: Several instances need one shared session store, one shared signing key and synced clocks; a cross-origin fetch sends cookies only with credentials.

content.statement: POST is an idempotent HTTP method, so sending the same POST /orders twice creates only one order.

remember: POST is not idempotent: each repeat may create another order, so retrying it needs a guard such as an idempotency key.

content.prompt: Each request is sent twice in a row. Match it with the result on the server.

right.text: User 5 no longer exists
Two new users named Ana exist
User 5 is named Ana
Nothing has changed

remember: GET, PUT and DELETE end in the same state however often they repeat; every repeated POST can create one more resource.

content.prompt: A checkout charged a customer twice. Order the events that led to it.

steps.text: The app sees a timeout and sends the same POST again
The server charges the card and sends 201
The app sends POST /payments
The server charges the card a second time
The 201 is lost when the phone drops its connection

remember: A timeout does not mean the request failed: the server may already have done the work, so a blind retry of a POST repeats it.

content.statement: If the client picks the order number and a unique index covers it, a retried create-order request cannot insert a second order row.

remember: A unique index on a client-chosen id turns a duplicate create into a conflict; answer it with the existing order instead.

content.prompt: An app retries DELETE requests after a timeout. Which endpoint can remove more than the user meant when a retry repeats a request the server already handled?

options.text: DELETE /cart/items/42, answering 404 once the item is gone
DELETE /sessions/current, signing out the caller's session
DELETE /cart/items/newest, removing the item added last
DELETE /cart/items?sku=A1, removing every item with that SKU

remember: A DELETE stays idempotent only if its URL names one fixed resource; 'the newest item' points to a different one after each call.

content.prompt: A worker handles 'add 10 points' messages from an at-least-once queue and skips message ids already in processed_messages. Which design adds the points exactly once, even if the worker crashes at any moment?

options.text: Add the points and the message id in one transaction, then ack
Add the points and commit, then insert the message id and ack
Insert the message id and commit, then add the points and ack
Add the points, ack the message, then insert the message id

remember: Record the handled message id in the same transaction as the change, so a redelivered message was either fully applied or not at all.

content.prompt: In JavaScript, three of these statements leave user the same whether they run once or twice in a row. Which one does not?

items.text: user.tags.add("vip"), where tags is a Set
user.until = Math.max(user.until, deadline)
Object.assign(user, { plan: "pro" })
user.history.push("upgraded")

remember: Setting a field, adding to a set and taking a max are idempotent; appending to a list is not, so a retried append records the event twice.

content.prompt: Clients choose their own Idempotency-Key values, and a customer may pay the same amount twice on purpose. Fill the blank in this PostgreSQL table.
content.code:
CREATE TABLE idempotency_keys (
  account_id   bigint NOT NULL,
  idem_key     text   NOT NULL,
  request_hash text   NOT NULL,
  response     jsonb,
  PRIMARY KEY (____)
);

remember: Scope idempotency keys to the caller, so two customers who pick the same key never collide or see each other's stored response.

content.prompt: What does this print?

remember: A replayed key ignores the new body; store a hash of the request with the key and reject a reuse whose body differs.

content.prompt: The payment provider deduplicates charges by idempotencyKey. A retry must never charge twice, even if the server crashes between the charge and the insert. Find the bug.

fixes.text: Run the charge and the insert in one database transaction
Pass key instead of a random UUID as idempotencyKey
Create one UUID at startup and reuse it for every charge

remember: A database transaction cannot undo a charge at another service; send a key derived from the client's key so a retry reuses the first charge.

content.statement: In PostgreSQL, LIMIT 10 OFFSET 20 skips the first 20 rows and returns the next 10.

remember: OFFSET is how many rows to skip and LIMIT is how many to return, so LIMIT 10 OFFSET 20 is page 3 of 10-row pages.

content.prompt: In keyset (cursor) pagination, each response carries a nextCursor. What does it hold?

options.text: A marker of the last item sent; the next page starts after it
The number of the page the client should request next
The total number of items the whole list contains
How many rows the server should skip on the next call

remember: A cursor marks where the last page ended, so the next page continues right after that item instead of counting rows.

content.prompt: Three of these are drawbacks of offset pagination (LIMIT/OFFSET). Which one is a drawback of cursor pagination instead?

items.text: A row added before the current page makes the next page repeat one
A row deleted from an earlier page makes the next page skip one
Page 5000 is slow because the skipped rows are still read
The client cannot jump straight from page 1 to page 50

remember: Offset pages drift when rows change and slow down deep in the list; cursor pages stay correct and fast but cannot jump to page N.

content.prompt: In ?page=2&size=20 the page number starts at 1. Fill the blank so each page starts at the right item.

remember: With page numbers that start at 1 the offset is (page - 1) * size; page * size skips the whole first page.

content.prompt: In Python 3, a job handles pending rows page by page, and a handled row stops being pending. What does this print?
content.code:
pending = list(range(1, 11))  # ids 1..10 are pending
done = []
offset = 0
while True:
    page = pending[offset:offset + 3]
    if not page:
        break
    for i in page:
        done.append(i)
        pending.remove(i)  # no longer pending
    offset += 3
print(done)

remember: If handling a page removes rows from the filtered list, a growing OFFSET skips rows; keep the offset at 0 or use a cursor.

content.prompt: Posts come in pages of size, each page continuing right after the last post of the page before. One post goes missing at every page boundary. Find the bug.

fixes.text: Compute has_more as len(rows) == size
Take the cursor from items[-1] instead of rows[-1]
Pass size instead of size + 1 as the LIMIT

remember: When you fetch size + 1 rows to detect a next page, build the cursor from the last row you return, not from the extra one.

content.prompt: Match each pagination technique with its trade-off.

right.text: Shows 'page 3 of 120', but must visit every matching row
Server may change what it encodes without breaking clients
Can jump to page 40, but deep pages get slower
Fast at any depth, but cannot jump to page 40

remember: Offset can jump but slows down deep, keyset stays fast but only steps along, opaque cursors hide their format, and totals cost a full count.

content.prompt: A job copies a huge, growing orders table to a warehouse in keyset batches. The checkpoint lives in a separate file, and a crash must never skip rows. Order one batch.

steps.text: Commit the warehouse transaction
Select WHERE id > checkpoint ORDER BY id LIMIT 1000
Save the batch's highest id as the new checkpoint
Read the checkpoint id saved by the last finished batch
Upsert the rows into the warehouse by id

remember: Advance a batch checkpoint only after the batch is committed; a crash then repeats a batch, which an upsert absorbs, instead of skipping it.

content.statement: In PostgreSQL, WHERE (score, id) < (:score, :id) gives the next keyset page for ORDER BY score DESC, id ASC.

remember: A row comparison like (a, b) < (x, y) fits only a sort where every column goes the same way; mixed directions need an explicit OR.

content.prompt: A client pages through tasks with a keyset cursor on (updated_at, id), newest first. While it reads page 2, someone edits a task that was on page 5. What happens to that task?

options.text: It appears twice, on page 3 and again on page 5
It appears on page 5 as planned, with its new values
It appears at the top of page 3, as the newest task
It is skipped, because it now sorts ahead of the cursor

remember: Keyset pagination on a column that changes, like updated_at, skips rows that move ahead of the cursor while a client is paging.

content.statement: A client that gets 429 Too Many Requests should resend the same request immediately.

remember: After a 429, wait as long as Retry-After says before trying again; instant retries only add load and fail again.

content.prompt: Each client should get its own 100 requests per minute, but once one busy client hits the limit, other clients calling the same URL get 429 too. Find the bug.

fixes.text: Raise LIMIT so busy clients reach it later
Use req.ip as the key instead of req.path
Return 503 instead of 429 when n > LIMIT

remember: A rate limit counts per client, keyed on something like the IP, API key or user id; a shared key lets one client block everyone.

content.prompt: Match each part of a rate-limited API response with what it tells the client.

right.text: How many requests are left in this window
How many requests the window allows in total
The request was rejected for going over the limit
How long to wait before trying again

remember: 429 rejects the request, Retry-After says when to come back, and X-RateLimit-Limit and -Remaining show the quota and what is left of it.

content.prompt: An API allows 100 requests per minute per API key. Order what a fixed-window limiter does with a client's 101st request this minute.

steps.text: Add one to the counter
Answer 429 with Retry-After set to the seconds left
Read the API key to identify the client
See that the new count is above 100
Look up the key's counter for the current minute

remember: A limiter identifies the client, counts the request in the current window, and answers 429 with Retry-After once the count passes the limit.

content.statement: Behind a single reverse proxy, a limiter keyed on the TCP connection's source IP puts all users into one shared limit.

remember: Behind a proxy every connection comes from the proxy's IP; key the limit on the forwarded client IP or on the user instead.

content.prompt: Your API runs 4 instances behind a round-robin load balancer. Each instance keeps its own in-memory limit of 100 requests per minute per API key. How many can one key get per minute?

remember: Separate in-memory counters multiply the limit by the number of instances; keep the counter in a shared store such as Redis.

content.prompt: 10,000 mobile clients got 429 with Retry-After: 60 at the same moment. Exactly 60 s later they all retry and are rejected again. What client change helps most?

options.text: Retry every second until one request succeeds
Wait Retry-After minus a fixed 5-second margin
Send the retry on a fresh connection right away
Wait Retry-After plus a random extra delay

remember: Add random jitter to retry delays so clients rejected together do not all come back at the same instant.

content.prompt: Three of these rate-limit keys let one client get around its limit. Which one does not?

items.text: Left-most entry of the X-Forwarded-For header
Entry your load balancer appended to X-Forwarded-For
Full IPv6 address of each request
Session id given to each new anonymous visitor

remember: Key limits on what the client cannot reset: the IP your own proxy recorded, an IPv6 /64 or an account, not client-sent headers or new sessions.

content.prompt: With Redis, each client may send 100 requests per 60-second window that starts at its first request. Fill the blank.

remember: With INCR and EXPIRE, set the TTL only when the count is 1; refreshing it on every request keeps a steady client's window from ever ending.

content.prompt: This token bucket serves a client that keeps retrying every 0.5 s after hitting the limit. What does this print?

remember: If rejected requests also spend tokens, a client retrying faster than the refill rate never gets through again.

content.statement: A cache hit means the requested value was already in the cache, so the slow source was not asked.

remember: A hit is served straight from the cache; a miss means the value must first be loaded from the slower source.

content.prompt: A value is stored in the cache with a TTL of 300 seconds. What does the TTL mean?

options.text: The value can be read from the cache at most 300 times
The cache fetches a fresh copy from the database every 300 seconds
After 300 seconds the value expires and is loaded again when needed
The database must answer the query within 300 seconds

remember: TTL (time to live) is how long a cached value may be served; once it runs out, the next request loads a fresh copy.

content.prompt: GET /api/me returns the signed-in user's profile. A developer caches the response under the key "me" for 60 seconds. What happens?

options.text: Users are shown the profile of whoever filled the cache
Each user sees their own profile, at most 60 seconds old
Every request misses because the key changes per user
The cache keeps one entry per user and fills up memory

remember: A cache key must include everything the response depends on, such as the user id, or one user's data is served to others.

content.prompt: Three of these can be served from a cache a few minutes stale without harm. Which one cannot?

items.text: The list of countries on the sign-up form
The categories shown in the shop menu
The 'most read this week' list on a blog
The balance checked before approving a withdrawal

remember: Cache data that may be a little stale; values a money or safety decision depends on are read fresh from the source.

content.prompt: Unknown ids are cached as null so bots probing random ids stop reaching the database. Fill the blank so a cached null counts as a hit.

remember: When you cache 'not found' as null, tell a miss from a hit by checking for undefined; a truthiness check treats the cached null as a miss.

content.prompt: This cache holds at most two entries. What does this print?

remember: An LRU cache evicts the entry used least recently, so reading a key protects it; a Map keeps insertion order, which makes it easy to build one.

content.prompt: Members get 10% off; everyone else pays the list price. After a few member visits, every customer sees ever lower prices. Find the bug.

fixes.text: Give the cache entry a TTL of 60 seconds
Declare product with let so it is a local copy
Return product.price * 0.9 instead of assigning it

remember: An in-process cache hands out the same object to every caller; treat cached values as read-only or copy them before changing anything.

content.prompt: Match each production cache problem with the fix that targets it.

left.text: Keys cached together at startup all expire in the same second
Bots request ids that exist in neither the cache nor the database
One very popular key overloads the cache node that holds it
During a rolling deploy, old code fails to read objects cached by new code

right.text: Keep a short-lived copy in each app server's memory
Add a random spread to each TTL
Put a format version in every cache key
Cache the not-found result for a short time

remember: Jitter TTLs against mass expiry, cache not-found results for missing ids, copy hot keys locally and version keys across deploys.

content.prompt: A hot key has just expired and many requests miss it at once. Order what the one request that rebuilds it does while the others wait.

steps.text: Release the rebuild lock
Look up the key and get a miss
Load the value from the database and cache it with a TTL
Take a rebuild lock that expires by itself after a few seconds
Read the cache again in case another request just filled it

remember: Rebuild a hot key under a lock that expires on its own, check the cache again once you hold it, and release it only after storing the value.

content.statement: In cache-aside, deleting the key right after the database commit guarantees no reader can put the old value back into the cache.

remember: A reader that loaded the old row before the commit can still store it after your delete, so keep a TTL as the backstop.

content.statement: Once the API puts a 'send welcome e-mail' job on a queue and responds, the e-mail has already been sent.

remember: Enqueueing only records the job; a worker does the work later, so the response cannot promise it is already done.

content.prompt: What does this print?

remember: The request only enqueues and answers; the worker runs the jobs afterwards, oldest first.

content.prompt: The queue retries a job only when its handler throws. While the mail server was down, failed welcome e-mails were logged but never retried. Find the bug.

fixes.text: Return false from the catch block to mark a failure
Add throw err; after the log line so the job fails
Move the user lookup inside the try block too

remember: A job that catches and logs its own error looks successful to the queue; rethrow so the queue can retry it.

content.prompt: Match each situation with the background-job feature that handles it.

left.text: Delete unconfirmed accounts every night at 03:00
Remind a user 24 hours after they abandon a cart
The mail server is down for a few minutes
A job failed all 5 attempts and needs a human to look

right.text: Dead-letter queue
Recurring (cron) job
Delayed job
Retry with exponential backoff

remember: Cron jobs run on a schedule, delayed jobs run once later, backoff rides out outages, and a dead-letter queue keeps jobs that never succeeded.

content.prompt: A deploy sends SIGTERM to a queue worker. Order what the worker does to shut down without losing jobs.

steps.text: Close the database and queue connections
Put jobs that are still unfinished back on the queue
Stop fetching new jobs from the queue
Exit the process
Wait up to the grace period for running jobs to finish

remember: On SIGTERM a worker stops fetching, lets running jobs finish, requeues the rest, then closes connections and exits.

content.statement: If three workers take jobs from one queue, two jobs enqueued for the same user can finish in the reverse order.

remember: Parallel workers can finish jobs in any order; if one job depends on another, chain them or send them through one worker.

content.prompt: Shipping-notice jobs often wait an hour in the queue, and support may fix the address meanwhile. The e-mail must show the current address. What goes in the job payload?

options.text: The whole order object, serialized when the job is enqueued
The finished e-mail HTML, rendered when the job is enqueued
The order id and the address, to save the worker a query
The order id; the worker loads the order when it runs

remember: Put ids in job payloads and load fresh data when the job runs; a snapshot taken at enqueue time can be stale by then.

content.prompt: At 02:00, 50,000 charge jobs fail together while the payment API is down. They retry after 1, 2, 4 and 8 minutes, and each wave knocks the API over again. What fixes this?

options.text: Add more workers so each retry wave finishes sooner
Retry every job after a fixed 1-minute delay instead
Add random jitter to each job's retry delay
Raise the maximum number of retry attempts per job

remember: Exponential backoff alone keeps jobs that failed together in step; random jitter spreads their retries out.

content.prompt: Three of these can make the same work run twice. Which one cannot?

items.text: The worker crashes after the work but before acking the job
The worker acks the job, then crashes midway through the work
A job runs longer than the queue's visibility timeout
An enqueue call times out after it succeeded and is retried

remember: Acking after the work risks duplicates; acking before the work risks losing the job, never running it twice.

content.prompt: In PostgreSQL, many workers run this at once. Fill the blank so each claims a different job without waiting for or failing on rows others have locked.
content.code:
UPDATE jobs SET status = 'running'
WHERE id = (
  SELECT id FROM jobs
  WHERE status = 'queued'
  ORDER BY id
  LIMIT 1
  ____
)
RETURNING id;

remember: In PostgreSQL, FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED lets many workers claim different queued rows at once without blocking each other.
